rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2.1-2.3 and Section 3 - the authors report their own airborne hyperspectral and thermal campaigns over 27 olive orchards in Spain and Italy (2011-2017), field disease-severity assessments of thousands of trees confirmed by PCR, and their own three-stage random-forest/spectral-clustering model whose outputs are evaluated against field-assessed symptomatic/asymptomatic status (Figs. 10-11).
rows.notes: The study is primary, but it only shows that airborne hyperspectral and thermal traits can detect Xf- and Vd-infected olive trees and discriminate between the two pathogens (OA 92-98%, kappa 0.7-0.8, FP 4-9%). It reports no result on controlling or limiting the expansion of Xylella fastidiosa, which is the function (pest_control) attributed to the passage; detection/discrimination is only a precondition for control. The study also does not itself demonstrate early (pre-visual) detection: it works on symptomatic trees (DS>=1) and explicitly lists early-stage detection as future work. Eradication/control benefits are mentioned only as motivation in the Introduction and Conclusions, not as own findings.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Study concerns remote-sensing detection and discrimination of two olive pathogens; no treatment, control intervention, or disease-spread outcome is measured.
